ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the figure, this is a circular-ring power generation device. A conducting rod with resistance R=4 Ω is bent into a closed circular ring with radius L=0.2 m, and the center of the circle is O. COD is a diameter, and a load resistor R1=1 Ω is connected between O and D. In the entire circular ring there is a uniform magnetic field B=0.5 T passing perpendicularly through the ring surface. The conducting rod OA with resistance r=1 Ω moves uniformly while touching the circular ring, with angular velocity ω=300 rad/s. When OA reaches OC, what is the electric power of the circular ring in W?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a circular-ring device. The circular ring is drawn as an ellipse, and the center is marked as O; the left end of the dashed horizontal diameter is marked as C, and the right end is marked as D, indicating that C, O, and D are on the same diameter. In the figure, a load resistor R1 is connected between O and D through an externally connected wire. The conducting rod OA points from O to a point A on the circular ring, and its own resistance r is marked. The question asks about the situation when OA turns to the OC position; at this time the outer end of the rod is connected to the left end C of the circular ring. Reasoning: When OA reaches OC, the two ends of the moving rod are O and C. The external circuit from C to D can pass along the upper and lower semicircular branch circuits of the circular ring; the total resistance of the circular ring is R=4 Ω, so the resistance of each semicircular branch circuit is R/2=2 Ω, and the parallel equivalent of the two branch circuits is 2 Ω ∥ 2 Ω=1 Ω. Then from D to O it still has to pass through the load R1=1 Ω, so the external resistance seen by the moving rod is 1 Ω+1 Ω=2 Ω. The motional electromotive force produced by the moving rod rotating uniformly about O is ε=BL²ω/2=0.5×0.2²×300/2=3 V. The moving rod's own resistance is r=1 Ω, so the total resistance of the whole circuit is 1 Ω+2 Ω=3 Ω, and the total current is I=ε/Rtotal=3/3=1 A. The problem asks for the electric power of the circular ring, including only the consumed electric power of the two semicircular branch circuits of the circular ring. The equivalent resistance of the circular-ring part is 1 Ω, so Pcircular ring=I²Rcircular ring=1²×1=1 W. Equivalently, the current in each of the two identical semicircular branch circuits is 0.5 A, and the power is 2×(0.5²×2)=1 W.
